passages.t: Molech, mediums, and the God who makes holy
passages.happening:
“Any Israelite or foreigner living in Israel who gives any of his children to Molech must be put to death. The people of the land are to stone him” (verse 2). God says, “I will set My face against that man and cut him off from his people” (verse 3). If the people look away and do nothing, God himself will act against the man and against all who follow him (verses 4-5).

The same is said of anyone who turns to mediums or spiritists (verse 6).

“Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, because I am the LORD your God. And you shall keep My statutes and practice them. I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 18 said what must not be done. Chapter 19 showed what a holy life looks like. Chapter 20 answers the question every body of law must answer: what happens when the commands are broken? Its tone is stern, and a modern reader feels it.

It does not begin with sex. It begins with children. The first and longest law is against giving a child to Molech, the rite in which children were killed. Of all the wrongs in this chapter, this is the one God names first.

Notice verses 4 and 5. The community may ‘hide their eyes’. People may know what a neighbor has done to his child and decide not to see it. God says that he sees, and that he will not let it pass. A society's silence about harm done to children is itself named as a wrong.

‘The people of the land’ were the free citizens of the community. Punishment was carried out by them together, which made everyone answerable for it.

Then, among the penalties, a different note: ‘I am the LORD who sanctifies you’. To sanctify is to make holy. Israel is told to be holy, and in the same breath told that God is the one who makes it so.
passages.later:
Israel's own kings did what this law forbids. Of King Manasseh it is written, “He sacrificed his own son in the fire, practiced sorcery and divination, and consulted mediums and spiritists” (2 Kings 21:6). His people did not hold him to this law, and the prophets counted such acts among the sins that led to exile.

Deuteronomy joins the same two things, child sacrifice and consulting the dead, in one list (Deuteronomy 18:10-11).

Jesus spoke of children in the strongest terms: “whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me” (Matthew 18:5).
passages.asks: God warned a whole community against hiding its eyes from what was done to a child. Ask whether there is harm to a child, or to anyone who cannot speak for themselves, that you or your church have found it easier not to see. And if you know of such harm now, tell someone who can act.

passages.happening:
“If anyone curses his father or mother, he must be put to death” (verse 9).

Death is set as the penalty for adultery, for both the man and the woman (verse 10); for a man who lies with his father's wife or his daughter-in-law (verses 11-12); and for sexual acts with an animal (verses 15-16). “If a man lies with a man as with a woman, they have both committed an abomination. They must surely be put to death; their blood is upon them” (verse 13).

Other acts carry other penalties. A man who marries his sister, and a man who lies with a woman during her period, are to be ‘cut off’ (verses 17-18). Of a man who takes his uncle's wife or his brother's wife it is said, ‘they shall be childless’ (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
Most of the acts named here were forbidden in chapter 18. This chapter sets penalties beside them. It is written as case law: if someone does this, this follows.

These verses should be read soberly. They were the law of an ancient people under God, decided by judges and witnesses. They are not a pattern for anyone today to take into their own hands, and they give no one permission to harm a child who disobeys.

Some things help a reader see what the passage is and is not.

The penalties are graded. Some acts carry death at the hands of the community. Others are left to God, who will ‘cut off’ the offender or leave a couple childless. The law does not treat every wrong alike.

‘Curses his father or mother’ does not mean a moment of rudeness or a child's bad temper. As in Exodus, it means rejecting one's parents or calling down harm on them.

The words ‘their blood is upon them’ meant that the guilt for the death lay with the offenders. Those who carried out the sentence were not counted as having shed blood.

How often these sentences were carried out is not clear. Israel's history tells of adulterers, King David among them, who were not put to death. One law says that no payment may be taken in place of a murderer's life, and some scholars think this implies that other death sentences could be set aside for a payment. On that reading, the penalty showed how grave the act was more than it fixed what must happen in every case. By the time of the Mishnah, around AD 200, Jewish courts had surrounded such cases with so many safeguards that an execution was rare. One saying there calls a court that put one person to death in seven years ‘destructive’.

Israel's neighbors also set death as the penalty for grave wrongs. This chapter differs in what it counts most serious: the killing of children first, then wrongs against parents and against the bonds of the family.
passages.later:
The law required witnesses for any sentence of death: “On the testimony of two or three witnesses a man shall be put to death, but he shall not be executed on the testimony of a lone witness” (Deuteronomy 17:6).

When the prophet Nathan faced David with his adultery, David said, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan answered, “The LORD has taken away your sin”, and added, “You will not die” (2 Samuel 12:13).

The Gospel of John tells of a woman caught in adultery and brought to Jesus. The passage is missing from many early copies of John, though the church has long treasured it. Jesus said, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7). When her accusers had gone, he said, “Then neither do I condemn you”, and, “Now go and sin no more” (John 8:11).

When Paul met a case of incest in the church at Corinth, he quoted the law's own formula, “Expel the wicked man from among you” (1 Corinthians 5:13). He meant removal from the fellowship of the church, in hope of the man's return, and not death.
passages.hard:
How should a reader today understand laws that set death as the penalty for adultery, for cursing parents and for sexual acts, including the acts of verse 13?

The penalties are severe by any modern measure, and it is honest to say so.

Christians give several answers, and they overlap. Many stress that these laws were given to Israel as a nation under God's direct rule, where the purity of the community was bound up with God's living among them. They were never given as a pattern for other nations. Christians have generally held that the moral wrongs named here remain wrong, while the penalties belonged to Israel's civil law and are not carried into the church. The church disciplines by setting a person outside its fellowship and by restoring them. It does not put anyone to death. A small number of Christian thinkers have argued that these penalties should still guide the laws of states. Most Reformed churches, among whom the view arose, have rejected it.

On verse 13: it repeats the law of 18:22 and adds the penalty. The note on 18:19-23 sets out how Christians read that law, the historic reading and the other, each in the words of those who hold it, and takes no side. Whatever a reader concludes there, the penalty of this verse belongs to the laws just described. It is no part of the church's teaching or practice, and it gives no person and no government a warrant to harm anyone.

So it must be said plainly. No one may use these verses to harm or shame any person, or to threaten, strike or kill. No one may use them to turn a son or daughter out of a home. Anyone who quotes this chapter to justify violence is misusing it. In the one scene where such a sentence was brought to Jesus, he stopped it (John 8:7).

If you are gay, or love someone who is, you are met with respect here. If these verses weigh on you, talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jesus turned a sentence of death into a question for the accusers: which of you is without sin? Ask which sins of other people you are quickest to condemn, and which of your own you pass over. And ask whether anyone has reason to be afraid of you because of what you believe.

passages.t: Set apart to be God's own
passages.happening:
“You are therefore to keep all My statutes and ordinances, so that the land where I am bringing you to live will not vomit you out” (verse 22). Israel is not to follow the ways of the nations before it (verse 23).

“I am the LORD your God, who has set you apart from the peoples” (verse 24). So Israel is to tell clean animals from unclean (verse 25). “You are to be holy to Me because I, the LORD, am holy, and I have set you apart from the nations to be My own” (verse 26).

The chapter ends with a last law: a man or woman who is a medium or spiritist is to be put to death (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
After the penalties comes the purpose. The chapter is framed, at start and finish, by laws against turning to other powers, and in the middle of that frame stand two calls to be holy.

Verse 26 is the goal. God has set Israel apart ‘to be My own’. The stern laws of this chapter are the reverse side of a belonging. Israel is to be different because it is his.

These verses also explain the food laws of chapter 11. God has told Israel apart from the nations, so Israel is to tell clean animals from unclean. Every meal was a small picture of whose people they were.

The warning about the land repeats chapter 18. It is spoken to Israel. The standard that fell on the nations before will fall on Israel too. These notes say nothing against any people, ancient or modern. The peoples named here are not a name for anyone living today, and this passage gives no one permission to hate or harm any people or to claim any land.

The law of verse 27 has a dark history in Christian hands. In early modern Europe and in colonial America, including the Salem trials of 1692, a verse like it in Exodus was cited to justify putting to death people accused of witchcraft. Most of them were women, and many were plainly innocent. That was a misuse of Scripture, and it was wrong. No one may use this verse to accuse, harm or drive out any person.
passages.later:
Peter takes the words of verse 26 and gives them to the church: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).

When Peter was shown a vision of clean and unclean animals together, he learned what the old line between them had pictured, and what had changed: “God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean” (Acts 10:28).

The prophet Ezekiel states what God wants in the end: “For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death, declares the Lord GOD. So repent and live” (Ezekiel 18:32).
passages.asks: God set a people apart ‘to be My own’. Ask whether you think of holiness first as a list of things forbidden, or as belonging to someone. And ask what in your life shows, to anyone watching, whose you are.
